F reaches B, C and D in one hop and every other node in at most three, so it scores 0.80, ahead of E 0.57 and G 0.44." width="100%"} Closeness measures how few steps a node needs to reach the rest of a bipartite graph. For each node in the chosen partition, the method adds up the hop-count distances (edge weights are ignored) to every node it can reach, on either side, and returns `(m + 2 * (n - 1)) / total`, where `n` is the size of the chosen partition and `m` the size of the other. That numerator is the smallest total a node on this side can have: a node next to every node on the other side is one step from each of them and two from each node on its own side, and it scores `1.0`. Nodes that need longer paths score lower. This is the normalization of Borgatti and Halgin, and the scores match those of NetworkX's `bipartite.closeness_centrality()`. The partitions are those returned by `bipartite_sets()`. Plain closeness would mark every node down for the steps through the other side that every path between two nodes of the same kind must take. Measuring against the best case for a bipartite graph removes that, which suits questions like: - which members can reach all events through the fewest intermediaries? - which papers are closest to the whole community of authors? - which diseases are most directly connected to the full set of genes? Only nodes in the chosen partition are scored. In a disconnected graph, the total covers only the nodes a node can reach, and the score is then multiplied by the share of the other nodes that it can reach, so nodes in small components score lower. A node that can reach no other node scores `0.0`. The method runs a graph traversal from every node in the chosen partition, so its cost grows roughly with the size of that partition times the size of the graph. On directed graphs edge direction is ignored, so distances are those of the underlying undirected graph. The whole graph is used and the current selection is ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [which]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which partition to compute centrality for: `0` (default) or `1`. Partitions are numbered as in `bipartite_sets()`: in each connected component, partition `0` is the side that contains the component's lowest node ID. Any other value raises an error. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node DataFrame column the scores are written to. If `None` (default), the column is named `"bipartite_closeness_centrality"`. Only nodes in the chosen partition are written: if the column is new, the other nodes get null values; if it already exists, their existing values are kept. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `False` (default), returns the graph itself so calls can be chained, and records the computation so it is listed by `describe()`. If `True`, returns the scores as a dictionary instead, without writing anything to the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping each node ID in the chosen partition to its closeness score (range `[0, 1]`). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): the graph itself, for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not bipartite, or if `which=` is not `0` or `1`. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~bipartite_degree_centrality`) : Rank the nodes of one side by their number of neighbors. [](`~bipartite_betweenness_centrality`) : Rank the nodes of one side by the paths through them. [](`~closeness_centrality`) : The same idea for any graph. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Ben is next to both clubs and two steps from each other person, the shortest distances possible, so he scores 1. Ana's distances to the other four nodes add up to 10 instead of 6, for a score of 0.6: ::: {#b1d1d501 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("Ana", "Chess"), ("Ben", "Chess"), ("Ben", "Choir"), ("Cruz", "Choir")] ) closeness = graph.bipartite_closeness_centrality( which=0, return_dict=True ) {graph.get_label_from_id(n): c for n, c in sorted(closeness.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'Ana': 0.6, 'Ben': 1.0, 'Cruz': 0.6} ``` ::: ::: ### Reaching every woman `davis_southern_women()` links 18 women in a town of the US South in the 1930s to the 14 social events (E1 to E14) each of them attended, and the `bipartite` attribute marks the two sides. E8, which 14 of the 18 women attended, is one step from each of them, two from every other event and three from the other four women, the closest of all the events: ::: {#e10cb029 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} davis = ec.davis_southern_women() closeness = davis.bipartite_closeness_centrality( which=1, return_dict=True ) ranked = sorted(closeness, key=closeness.get, reverse=True) [(davis.get_label_from_id(n), round(closeness[n], 3)) for n in ranked[:3]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [('E8', 0.846), ('E9', 0.786), ('E7', 0.733)] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#bd0d622b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} women, events = davis.bipartite_sets() davis.set_node_attrs("closeness", closeness).layout_bipartite( nodes=women, aspect_ratio=0.5 ).plot( layout="pos", color_by="closeness", color_scale="sequential", label_by="label", height=900, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
